newsitem.title: UK: Sheep-cloners PPL to breed for transplants.
newsitem.headline: Sheep-cloners PPL to breed for transplants.

text.p: PPL Therapeutics Plc , which created a global furore earlier this month by cloning an adult sheep, plans to get into the equally controversial business of animal-to-human transplants, managing director Ron James said on Monday.

James said PPL would start research on genetically engineering pigs for use in xenotransplants. The research is likely to concentrate on pig's hearts, as they are a good match for humans in terms of size and function.

James, who was briefing reporters on PPL's first annual results, for 1996, said the technology suited the company. PPL specialises in creating transgenic animals, which have some human genes and can produce human proteins in their milk.

James said the same technology could be used to create pigs that produce human sugars on the surfaces of their organs. These sugars help the immune system identify foreign agents, so pig organs that produced human sugars would theoretically be recognised as human and not be rejected.
Such pigs have already been created by other companies. But PPL's cloning technology could be used to grow cloned transgenic pigs -- saving a step in the production process.

Now hit-and-miss genetic engineering must be used to insert human genes into a pig cell. If it takes, that pig is then bred. Cloning theoretically allows for a herd of successfully engineered animals to be grown immediately.
The British government has declared a moratorium on xenotransplants until all the dangers, such as introducing an unknown virus into people, are studied. But James said this would not affect PPL.

"By the time we get around to trials either the moratorium will have been lifted or we will be able to do them somewhere else," he said. James said he suspected some other company, such as Cambridge-based Imutran, owned by Novartis, would be in trials first.
James also said PPL would support its research partner, the Roslin Institute.

Just as PPL and Roslin announced they had cloned an adult sheep, the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (MAFF) said it was cutting funding for the project by 50 percent this year and 100 percent next year. Roslin says the government package was worth 600,000 pounds ($976,000).
"If MAFF isn't prepared to fund it then PPL and others are prepared to fund it," James said.
He said they would not fund agricultural research, however. Roslin was first set up to study better ways of rearing farm
